meta.title: AI Law & Regulation Radar
meta.note: Curated current AI legal and regulatory developments across the EU, Ireland, US and Nigeria, plus Nigerian Bar Association / profession updates and notable AI court cases. Refreshed daily by a scheduled task. Summaries are original; follow the source link for detail.

items.title: SI 2026/425 in force: ICO now under statutory duty to write an AI/ADM Code of Practice
items.summary: The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/425), in force since 12 May 2026, put the Information Commissioner under a fresh statutory duty (new s.124A DPA, inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025) to produce a formal Code on AI and ADM, with a mandatory children's-data component — a 17 August advisory flags this as arguably the most significant AI instrument the ICO has yet been handed. The ICO's own draft ADM guidance (consultation closed 29 May) previews the direction ahead of final guidance expected this summer and the statutory Code itself in 2027; once finalised, the Code carries the same weight as the Children's Code — courts must have regard to it, and so must the ICO in enforcement. Crucially it catches deployers, not just developers: any organisation using a third-party AI/ADM tool on UK-connected individuals is in scope, including businesses with no UK presence at all where they offer AI-enabled goods/services to, or monitor, people in the UK. Practical read for the corridor and Aegis Guard's UK DUAA rule: this is the ICO formally signalling the enforcement benchmark that rule will eventually be measured against, and a live prompt to check any UK-facing client's recruitment/credit/HR AI tooling for 'meaningful human involvement' (active review, not token sign-off) now, well ahead of 2027.

items.title: California suspense file: AB 412 copyright bill dies, SB 813 AI safety body advances
items.summary: Sacramento's two appropriations committees ran their once-a-year 'suspense file' hearing on 13 August, deciding in under an hour which of roughly 30 pending AI bills live or die before the 31 August session close. AB 412, the AI Copyright Transparency Act (would have required generative-AI developers to document and disclose registered copyrighted training works to rightsholders on request, backed by SAG-AFTRA), was held in committee — dead for 2026 after industry argued full training-set disclosure was technically infeasible. SB 813, creating a California AI Standards and Safety Commission to recognise voluntary safety-certification bodies, passed 11-3 and moves to the Rules Committee, alongside its companion auditor-registry bill AB 1405; several child-safety chatbot bills (AB 2023/SB 1119, SB 867, SB 300) and deepfake/digital-replica bills (SB 1111, SB 1015) also advanced. Practical read: California's pattern of signing transparency/disclosure bills while killing ones that create hard liability (the same split seen with SB 53 and the vetoed SB 7/SB 1047) is repeating — useful US comparator when a client asks whether Article 50-style marking duties are becoming a global norm faster than EU-style training-data transparency obligations are.
items.source: Tech Times / California Senate & Assembly Appropriations Committees

items.title: NDPC opens forensic probe into UNILAG, Lotus Bank over students' data used to open accounts
items.summary: The Nigeria Data Protection Commission opened a forensic investigation on 14 August into the University of Lagos (UNILAG), Lotus Bank and fintech Hackerbella Ltd over allegations that students' personal data was used without lawful basis to open bank accounts on their behalf. NDPC's stated scope goes well beyond the underlying complaint: DPIAs, the lawfulness of any credit-scoring or profiling activity, use of automated decision-making systems, privacy notices, data-sharing arrangements, retention, and technical/organisational safeguards are all explicitly in scope, per NDPC head Dr Vincent Olatunji. Practical read: this is the NDPA 2023 machinery being used, in real time, against a university-fintech-bank data pipeline that profiles and scores individuals — directly on point for any Nigerian-corridor client running AI-driven credit scoring or onboarding on personal data sourced from a third party, and a live illustration of the automated-decision-making scrutiny the GAID 2025 Schedule 5 corridor work already tracks.

items.title: First real-world test of California's AI Transparency Act finds 6 of 13 covered companies non-compliant
items.summary: Investigative outlet Indicator, working with the nonprofit WITNESS, ran the first compliance test of California's AI Transparency Act (SB 942) and the EU's parallel Article 50 marking duty, both live since 2 August. Of the 13 major generative-AI providers in scope (1M+ California monthly users) — Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Adobe, Grok, Midjourney, Mistral, HeyGen, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, Suno, TikTok — only 7 had a working detector tool at all; of those, only Google's and OpenAI's correctly flagged AI origin after the file had been edited, with every other detector's accuracy degrading once content was tampered with. Non-compliance carries a $5,000-per-violation-per-day civil penalty under SB 942. Practical read: even the providers squarely big enough to be in scope of both SB 942 and Article 50 are shipping detection tools late or with real accuracy gaps — a useful, dated data point for any client weighing whether 'we'll build a detector eventually' is still a theoretical risk.

items.title: NIMC's new Root CA role for digital signatures risks colliding with the Digital Economy Bill
items.summary: A 13 August analysis flags a genuine drafting collision now that the NIMC Act 2026 (signed 26 June) makes the National Identity Management Commission Nigeria's Root Certification Authority — issuing root digital certificates and overseeing the trust framework for electronic signatures tied to the NIN. The still-pending National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill also legislates digital identity and e-signatures, and the two frameworks were drafted on separate tracks with no reconciliation. Practical read: any client relying on Nigerian e-signatures or NIN-linked digital identity for contract execution or AI-driven KYC should treat NIMC as the certificate authority of record now, but expect the Digital Economy Bill's eventual passage to force a second look at which regime actually governs — this is a live regulatory-overlap risk, not a settled point.

items.title: Colorado AG publishes draft ADMT & Chatbot Safety Act rules, comments open to 26 Oct
items.summary: The Colorado Department of Law filed draft rules implementing the revised Automated Decision-Making Technology Act (SB 26-189) and the new Chatbot Safety Act (HB 26-1263) with the Secretary of State on 11 August — both laws take effect 1 January 2027. The ADMT rules operationalise the scaled-back disclosure-and-rights framework (consumer notice, access, correction, human review) after May's amendment stripped out the original EU-style risk-management and impact-assessment duties; the Chatbot Safety Act rules cover age estimation, AI-disclosure to users, and self-harm response protocols for services engaging minors. Comments are open through 26 October, with a 5 October soft deadline to influence the rulemaking hearing. Directly relevant to the still-open Aegis Guard 'go global' item — this is the first concrete rule text to build a Colorado jurisdiction module against, materially different in shape from the EU/UK/Nigeria/Singapore/Egypt rules already live (disclosure-and-rights, not risk-tiered obligations).
items.source: Consumer Finance Monitor (Ballard Spahr) / Colorado Department of Law

items.title: Critics say AI Act's high-risk delay leaves migration and border AI unregulated
items.summary: A 6 August explainer traces what changed on 2 August and what didn't: Article 50 transparency duties are now enforceable, but the Digital Omnibus's push of Annex III high-risk obligations to December 2027 leaves AI systems used in migration, asylum and border management — already classified high-risk under Annex III — without the Act's risk-management, documentation and human-oversight requirements for another 16 months. Digital rights groups (Equinox Initiative for Racial Justice, the ProtectNotSurveil coalition) argue this widens existing non-discrimination gaps and raises the risk of wrongful asylum rejections, while EU-funded border-surveillance tech deployed outside the bloc sits outside the Act's reach altogether. Practical read: an Annex III migration/border client is still governed by GDPR and national law in the interim — the Act's own safeguards for that specific use case simply aren't live yet.

items.title: NITDA signs National Sovereign Cloud Initiative framework covering AI infrastructure
items.summary: NITDA signed three regulatory instruments on 5 August — the National Cloud Computing Guideline, National Cloud Technical Guideline and National Digital Infrastructure Assurance Framework — plus a National Cloud Investment Strategy, together forming Nigeria's National Sovereign Cloud Initiative. The framework explicitly names AI infrastructure and sovereign computing among the digital assets it's designed to govern, and NITDA plans to operationalise a national regulatory platform by October 2026 for onboarding, assessment and certification of cloud and digital infrastructure providers. For any client building or hosting AI systems on Nigerian infrastructure, this is a live, dated compliance track distinct from the still-pending Digital Economy Bill and NITDA's AI risk-classification regime — worth tracking as its own registration/certification obligation once the October platform goes live.

items.title: Consolidated AI Act text reveals AI Office's inspection, sealing and 5%-per-day penalty powers
items.summary: The consolidated Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 text (ref. 02024R1689-20260727, in force since 27 July, folding in the Digital Omnibus) reveals detail behind the headline 'enforcement starts 2 August' story: new Articles 75a-75d give the AI Office exclusive competence over two categories — GPAI-based systems where model and system share the same provider or undertaking, and AI systems that are or sit inside a Digital Services Act-designated very large online platform (Google Search, YouTube, Meta's platforms, TikTok, LinkedIn, Amazon, Bing among them). For those systems, enforcement moves entirely out of national regulators' hands to one Brussels office, which can now enter and seal premises, compel oral testimony, bill its own investigation costs back to a non-compliant operator once non-compliance is found, and impose periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of average daily turnover per day to force compliance — stacked on top of the existing €15M/3% and €35M/7% fine tiers. Practical read: for any client whose AI stack runs on or inside a designated VLOP, the live regulator relationship just narrowed from 'your national sectoral authority' to a single office with search-and-seal powers — worth a line in any Article 25(2) vendor-documentation clause.

items.title: AI Office of Ireland gets its board — Mary Doyle named chair, seven-person board confirmed
items.summary: DETE confirmed on 5 August that Mary Doyle — a former assistant/deputy secretary general across the Departments of the Taoiseach, Health and Education — will chair the AI Office of Ireland's board, a week after CEO Paul Byrne's appointment and the Office's establishment. The other six board seats are split between officialdom and subject expertise: Dept. of Enterprise principal officer Dr Michelle Kearney, chartered accountant Donal Rooney (Enterprise Ireland), Trinity law professor Deirdre Byrne, DCU emeritus computing professor Alan Smeaton, Shutterstock's AI/data-science director Dr Alessandra Sala, and Carne's chief data and AI officer Siobhan Noble. Practical read: the Office now has its full governance structure in place — CEO, chair and board — a week into its operational life as Ireland's central coordinating authority and single point of contact under the EU AI Act, closing what had been the last open leadership gap.

items.title: Munich court rules against Suno: AI training abroad no shield, EU AI Act compliance no defence
items.summary: The Munich District Court I ruled for GEMA against Suno on 31 July — Europe's first major AI-generated-music copyright judgment, and doctrinally sharper than the earlier GEMA v OpenAI decision (still on appeal). Three findings matter beyond music: the court took jurisdiction over training conduct that happened entirely in the US and then ran a full US fair-use analysis itself, finding Suno's case distinguishable from Bartz v Anthropic and Kadrey v Meta because the outputs were substantially similar to the originals; it held that memorisation of works inside a model hosted on German servers is itself an infringing reproduction, not just the output; and — most relevant to any provider leaning on Article 53(1)(c)-(d) — it held that EU AI Act copyright-policy and training-summary compliance does not shield a provider from copyright liability, reading Recital 107 as making enforcement easier for rightsholders, not harder. Not final (Suno can appeal, and the CJEU's Like Company opinion lands 3 September 2026), but the practical guidance for any client training or fine-tuning models is unchanged and now firmer: provenance and lawful data access are the exposure, and AI Act compliance paperwork is not a copyright defence.
items.source: Reed Smith (Munich District Court I, case no. 42 O 763/25)

items.title: White House finalises but withholds its voluntary frontier-AI model review framework
items.summary: President Trump's 2 June executive order (EO 14409) gave agencies 60 days — to 1 August — to build a voluntary process letting AI labs submit frontier models for government vetting before release. The deadline passed with nothing published; the White House then confirmed on 3 August the framework was in fact finished, but said it will not release the document or disclose which companies have seen it, reviewing the draft behind closed doors on 4 August with Meta, Nvidia, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic among others. Because the order explicitly bars the framework from operating as a mandatory licensing or preclearance requirement, participation is voluntary and enforcement leverage is unclear. Worth flagging to any US-facing client as a live contrast with the EU's own Code of Practice below — also voluntary, but published in full with a running signatory list: transparency of the rulebook itself, not just compliance with it, is now a live governance-design question on both sides of the Atlantic.

items.title: Commission confirms ~190 signatories to the AI-Generated Content Transparency Code ahead of Article 50
items.summary: The Commission confirmed on 31 July that roughly 190 organisations — including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Mistral and Cohere on the provider side, and deployers such as Getty Images, Lufthansa and Iberdrola — have signed the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content, the voluntary instrument operationalising Article 50's marking and labelling duties. About half the signatories are small or recently founded firms; the Commission's own framing is that signing gives a 'streamlined, predictable and legally certain pathway' to demonstrate compliance rather than having to prove it from scratch to a regulator. Two industry task forces launch in September 2026 to shape implementation, so signing now also buys a seat at that table. The list stays open and updates on a rolling basis (last updated 5 August) — worth checking again before advising a client the Code isn't relevant to their AI stack.
items.source: European Commission — Shaping Europe's Digital Future

items.title: California's AI Transparency Act (SB 942) goes operative, deliberately timed to the EU AI Act
items.summary: SB 942, as amended by AB 853, became operative on 2 August 2026 for 'covered providers' — generative AI systems with over one million California monthly users. From now those providers must offer a free public AI-content detection tool, let users add a visible AI disclosure to generated content, and embed a hidden machine-readable provenance watermark in AI-generated images, video and audio; the same disclosure duty extends to hosting platforms from 1 January 2027 and capture-device makers from 1 January 2028. Commentary is explicit that the operative date was moved to align with the EU AI Act's own 2 August enforcement start, so any provenance/watermarking build already done for Article 50 largely transfers — but the triggers differ (California is a one-million-user threshold, not an EU-market test), so scope has to be checked separately rather than assumed to mirror Article 50's coverage.
items.source: California SB 942 / AB 853 (Nat'l Law Review, Vorp Labs coverage)

items.title: Commission formally starts AI Act enforcement as Article 50 transparency rules go live
items.summary: The Commission's own press corner confirmed on 2 August that the AI Office, together with national authorities, has now begun enforcing the AI Act, with Article 50 transparency obligations applying from the same date: chatbots and other interactive systems must disclose they are AI, deepfakes must be labelled, and AI-generated or altered content must carry machine-readable marks. This is the formal 'switch is now on' statement to cite over the bare statutory date — useful alongside the 31 July AI Office staffing/whistleblower-tool item already tracked, since that covered the machinery being readied and this confirms it is now live. High-risk Annex III obligations are unaffected and remain deferred to 2 December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus.

items.title: EU AI Office adds 38 staff, launches whistleblower + compliance tools as enforcement starts
items.summary: The Commission's AI Office announced on 31 July it is adding 38 staff in Brussels to police AI Act compliance from 2 August, covering everyone from EU startups to OpenAI and DeepSeek. Alongside the headcount it switched on two new reporting channels: an AI Act Whistleblower Tool letting anyone professionally connected to a GPAI provider confidentially report harmful practices (legal retaliation protection under the Whistleblower Directive attaches from 2 August), and a separate Compliance Tool for users to flag suspected violations. Executive VP Henna Virkkunen framed it as the enforcement phase proper — investigators can now demand technical documentation, interview company staff, and pursue fines or market withdrawal. Useful to cite over the bare statutory date when a client asks what 'enforcement begins 2 August' actually looks like on the ground — this is the machinery being staffed, not just the law switching on.
items.source: Associated Press (via ABC News); AI Office Whistleblower Tool page confirms the mechanism

items.title: AI Office of Ireland formally established, Paul Byrne appointed as first CEO
items.summary: Ministers Peter Burke and Niamh Smyth confirmed on 30 July that Oifig IS na hÉireann (the AI Office of Ireland) is now formally established under the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026 (signed into law 21 July), with Paul Byrne — previously Executive Director at the Medical Council of Ireland and President of CLEAR, the international regulators' alliance — named as its first CEO. The Office is confirmed as a Market Surveillance Authority in its own right, acting as Single Point of Contact for the European Commission and coordinating the 15 sectoral regulators designated under S.I. 366/2025; it is on track to be operational by 2 August 2026, the same day GPAI enforcement and Article 50 transparency obligations bite. Practically, this closes the last open question on Ireland's enforcement architecture going into the 2 August deadline: there is now a named CEO and a confirmed statutory MSA role, not just a bill. Note DETE's own release flags further legislation coming in Autumn to give effect to Digital Omnibus amendments — worth revisiting then.
items.source: Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment

items.title: Germany's KI-MIG takes effect — BaFin gains AI enforcement power over banks and insurers
items.summary: Germany's AI Market Surveillance and Innovation Promotion Act (KI-MIG) entered into force on 29 July 2026, finally designating national AI Act enforcement authorities after Germany missed the EU's own August 2025 designation deadline: BaFin for financial services, the Bundesnetzagentur for the wider economy, with the BfDI retaining the GDPR overlay. BaFin's mandate is live now for Article 50 transparency (chatbot disclosure, enforceable from 2 August) and prohibited-practice violations (fines to €35M or 7% of turnover); the harder Annex III high-risk tier — credit scoring, insurance pricing — is deferred to December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus, consistent with the tracker's own Annex III date. The instructive detail for any regulatory-strategy conversation: commentary is already citing BaFin's Wirecard-era enforcement failures as reason to doubt a newly-armed regulator will use these powers early, versus the 18–24 month lag GDPR fines took to materialise after enforcement began. A useful comparator for how Ireland's own 15-regulator sectoral model may behave once its AI Office is live from 1 August.

items.title: Senate hearing advances bill forcing social media firms into Nigeria, plus an AI Academy bill
items.summary: The Senate ICT Committee held a public hearing on 24 July on two bills with direct AI-governance relevance: Sen. Ned Nwoko's bill amending the NDPA 2023 to require social media companies operating in Nigeria to maintain a physical local office (explicitly framed by its sponsor around AI research, compliance and trust-and-safety functions, citing Ireland's Big Tech hub model as the template Nigeria should emulate), and Sen. Yemi Adaramodu's bill establishing an AI Academy in Omuo-Ekiti, Ekiti State. Both cleared the hearing with Senate leadership backing and now move to committee report stage before a floor vote — a harder, better-sourced data point than the still-unconfirmed 'Digital Economy Bill has passed the Senate' claim already tracked from 21 July. For anyone advising platforms or AI vendors with a Nigerian user base, a physical-presence mandate routed through an NDPA amendment is a materially different compliance ask than the risk-classification regime NITDA has been drafting — worth tracking as its own legislative track, not a restatement of the Digital Economy Bill.

items.title: EDPB and Commission announce joint guidelines on GDPR–competition law interplay, Oct. consultation
items.summary: The EDPB and European Commission announced on 23 July a remote stakeholder consultation set for 15 October 2026 to inform joint guidelines on how data protection law and competition law interact — the second structured input session in a process tracing back to the CJEU's July 2023 Meta v Bundeskartellamt ruling, which let competition authorities weigh GDPR compliance in dominance cases provided they consult the lead DPA and are bound by its findings. The gap the guidelines are meant to close: what information the two regulator types can share, and which authority holds lead jurisdiction when the same data-harvesting conduct is both a privacy violation and a market-power abuse. For any client building AI products dependent on a dominant platform (data access, API terms, training-data supply), this is the direction EU enforcement is heading — a company will no longer be able to play a favourable DPA finding off against an unfavourable competition ruling on the same facts, or vice versa. No binding text yet; a formal call for expressions of interest is expected on the EDPB site in the coming weeks.
items.source: Tech Times / European Data Protection Board

items.title: OpenAI signs 88,000 sq ft Dublin EU HQ lease, 250 jobs, five days before AI Act fines go live
items.summary: OpenAI signed an 88,000 sq ft lease at Dublin's Tropical Fruit Warehouse on 27 July, tripling its Irish headcount to 350 and committing roughly €105M — five days before EU AI Act GPAI enforcement fines (up to €15M or 3% global turnover) go live on 2 August. The build-out matters more than the square footage: OpenAI Ireland Limited is the GDPR Article 56 lead-authority establishment for the whole EEA, and the EDPB's 2024 one-stop-shop tightening requires genuine EU decision-making authority, not a letterbox address — pairing Associate GC/Head of OpenAI Ireland Emma Redmond with a commercial lead as the two foundational hires is the tell. For Irish AI Act practice, this confirms the DPC and the AI Office of Ireland are now the live frontline enforcement relationship for the world's largest GPAI provider, not a theoretical one.

items.title: Digital Omnibus on AI formally published as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July
items.summary: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 — the Digital Omnibus on AI — was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July under an urgency procedure tied to the 2 August deadline. This gives a citable regulation number to what the tracker had flagged as provisional since 10 July: the Annex III high-risk deadline (2 Dec 2027) and Annex I deadline (2 Aug 2028) are now unconditional calendar dates, no longer contingent on the Commission's standards-readiness trigger. Any client-facing document still describing the Omnibus timeline as 'pending' or 'proposed' should be updated to cite Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 directly.
items.source: NicFab Blog (Digital Omnibus on AI, EU Official Journal)

items.title: President Connolly signs the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill 2026 into law
items.summary: President Catherine Connolly signed the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill 2026 on 21 July 2026, the final step after it completed Seanad Report and Final Stage on 15 July — Ireland's domestic AI Act enforcement architecture is now law, not just a bill in passage. The Act establishes Oifig IS na hÉireann (AI Office of Ireland) as the coordinating authority and single point of contact for the EU AI Act, on track for its 1 August 2026 operational deadline. Practical effect for anyone advising Irish-facing AI deployments: the 15-regulator sectoral model under S.I. 366/2025 (Central Bank, DPC, CCPC etc. as Market Surveillance Authorities) now has its statutory backbone in force, and the AI Office's coordination, registry and sandbox functions are no longer contingent on the Bill passing — they are a live legal obligation with 11 days to go before the Article 50 deadline.

items.title: France's competition authority: three firms hold 84% of the AI agents market
items.summary: The Autorité de la concurrence published Opinion 26-A-05 on 17 July 2026, its third AI market study after cloud computing and generative AI, this time examining agentic AI. Headline finding: OpenAI, Google and Anthropic together hold over 84% of the AI agent market, with lock-in risk compounding as agents become the primary interface between users and the wider digital economy — vertically integrated players who bundle agents into existing products (OS, browser, messaging) gain a structural advantage, and agentic commerce could send AI agents 20-25% of e-commerce traffic by 2030. The Authority stopped short of recommending new AI-specific rules, instead pushing for full use of existing competition law, the AI Act and the DMA, plus interoperability and data-portability commitments from operators. For any client building or procuring agentic AI tools, this is the first authority-level market-concentration data point on the sector — useful context alongside the CNIL/CIANum note on agentic AI and GDPR from three days earlier (20 July, already tracked), both signals that French regulators are treating agent autonomy as this year's live compliance and competition frontier.

items.title: Reported, unconfirmed: Senate committee chair says Digital Economy Bill has cleared the Senate
items.summary: At the T&A Legal AI Summit 2026 in Lagos, Senator Shuaib Afolabi Salisu — Chairman of the Senate Committee on ICT and Cybersecurity and the bill's lead sponsor — told the room that the National Digital Economy and e-Governance Bill 'has completed legislative processes in the Senate' and is expected to receive presidential assent, a step past the 'third reading' status ThisDayLive reported on 9 July. We checked this against the National Assembly's own Bill Tracker (Bill No. 11264, Senate, filed 13 July 2026) and all four reading stages show as 'Not Available' — a data gap on NASS's own site rather than evidence against the claim, consistent with the tracker's known unreliability. No second press outlet has yet reported Senate passage as complete either. Worth watching given the AI Office coordination this bill would enable, but hold it as reported by the sponsor rather than as confirmed fact until an official record catches up.
items.source: T&A Legal AI Summit 2026, via Governing Intelligence (Samideen Abdullateef) — Senate passage unconfirmed by NASS's own Bill Tracker

items.title: Regulation of AI Bill 2026 completes both Houses of the Oireachtas
items.summary: The Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill 2026 completed Seanad Report and Final Stage on 15 July 2026, finishing its full passage through both Houses of the Oireachtas after completing all Dáil stages between 24 and 30 June. The President's signature is the one remaining step before enactment. The Bill establishes Oifig IS na hÉireann (AI Office of Ireland), Ireland's central coordinating authority under the EU AI Act, due to be operational by 1 August 2026 — a deadline the completed parliamentary passage keeps on track.

items.title: Spain's Organic AI Governance Law: status check finds a slower Congress track
items.summary: Spain's Council of Ministers approved the draft Organic Law for the Good Use and Governance of Artificial Intelligence on 26 May 2026 and sent it to Congress, where it was published on 12 June and referred to the Committee on Economy, Trade and Digital Transformation. The Bill would implement Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 domestically, naming AESIA, the AEPD and the CGPJ as notifying and market-surveillance authorities, setting infringements and penalties, creating regulatory sandboxes, and requiring the public sector to register and publish its AI use. Its amendment window currently runs to 2 September 2026 per the Congress record — a materially slower track than Ireland (both Houses complete 15 July) or Greece (enacted 17 July), useful context when comparing Member State implementation readiness.

items.title: Spain's judicial council fines a judge over undisclosed use of ChatGPT in a draft ruling
items.summary: Spain's General Council of the Judiciary (CGPJ) fined a provincial court judge €1,000 after he used ChatGPT to draft the reasoned section of a ruling and left references to the tool in the final text, alerting colleagues to the AI's role. The Disciplinary Commission treated it as serious misconduct under judicial confidentiality rules, stopping short of the more severe charge of substituting judicial function — its reasoning was that the AI served as an aid and complement to the judge's own analysis, rather than a substitute for it. The decision applies the CGPJ's own instruction of 28 January 2026, which requires constant, real and effective human control over any AI input into issuing rulings, weighing facts or evidence, or applying the law. Understood to be Spain's first disciplinary sanction of its kind, and a concrete marker for how far 'human in the loop' has to go in a judicial setting.
items.source: Consejo General del Poder Judicial (via Infobae, Público)

items.title: AEPD publishes technical note on data quality and accuracy in AI processing
items.summary: Spain's data protection authority published a technical note on 21 July 2026 analysing how the GDPR's accuracy and minimisation principles apply to personal data processing that incorporates AI systems — one of the first systematic treatments of the question by any DPA, aimed at controllers, processors and DPOs. The core clarification: GDPR accuracy does not require data to be permanently truthful or up to date, only adequate to the purpose of the processing — an absolute reading would itself conflict with minimisation and create disproportionate burdens for AI development. Data quality has to be assessed at the level of the training dataset (representativeness, bias, relevance), not just each individual record, and separately again at the output stage — inferences, predictions and decisions must not misrepresent the people affected, with a higher bar wherever a result affects a specific individual. The AEPD also confirms synthetic data generation, anonymisation and bias correction are compatible with the accuracy principle provided they are justified by purpose and don't create adverse effects. Directly usable interpretive authority for any DPIA or AI governance programme built on GDPR Articles 5(1)(c)-(d).
items.source: Agencia Española de Protección de Datos

items.title: Greek Parliament passes law transposing the EU AI Act into national law
items.summary: Greece's Parliament passed legislation on 17 July 2026 — 'Measures for the Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 ... Amendment of Law 4961/2022' — making Greece one of the first Member States to complete its national AI Act implementing mechanism ahead of the 2 August deadline. The law designates the Hellenic Data Protection Authority as the central market surveillance body and the National Telecommunications and Post Commission (EETT) as notifying authority, operating a new AI Coordination and Expertise Center; it sets penalties for violations (including against public-sector bodies), creates a unified complaints system, introduces criminal penalties for stripping transparency labels off deepfake content, and establishes AI regulatory sandboxes. A useful comparator for Ireland's own S.I. 366/2025 multi-regulator model and the still-progressing Regulation of AI Bill 2026 — Greece has chosen a DPA-led single lead authority rather than Ireland's sectoral-regulator/coordinating-office split.

items.title: Poland's UODO calls for AI-in-employment rules to close a discrimination gap
items.summary: Poland's data protection authority President, Mirosław Wróblewski, wrote to the Ministry of Labour on 16 July 2026 urging new rules to protect job candidates and employees against discrimination from AI recruitment and workplace-monitoring tools, which he notes tend to entrench biases present in their training data and can process far more personal data — including special-category data — than the Labour Code's Article 22(1) permits an employer to request directly. He ties the request to the AI Act's own machinery: recruitment AI is Annex III high-risk, Article 86 already gives affected individuals a right to a meaningful explanation of a high-risk system's role in a decision, and Article 27's fundamental-rights impact assessment must run alongside — not instead of — a GDPR DPIA before any such system is deployed. UODO has offered the ministry technical support in drafting. Relevant precedent for any client building AI-driven HR or recruitment tooling for the EU market: a national DPA is actively pushing for stricter domestic guardrails on top of the AI Act baseline, not weaker ones.

items.title: Commission adopts Article 50 transparency guidelines — 12 days before the rules bite
items.summary: The European Commission adopted its guidelines on the transparency obligations for providers and deployers of AI systems on 20 July 2026 — the first Commission instrument interpreting the full scope of Article 50, covering chatbot disclosure, deepfake and synthetic-media labelling, and AI-generated text on matters of public interest. They are non-binding, but they define the scope competent authorities will read Article 50 against once the obligations apply on 2 August, and they land alongside the separately-assessed voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content (formally judged 'adequate' by the Commission this month). The practical read for anyone running a chatbot or shipping synthetic image, audio, video or text into the EU: the interpretive gaps you have been guessing at — what counts as a 'directly interactive' system, which disclosures sit with the provider versus the deployer, and the artistic and law-enforcement exceptions — now have an official answer, and you have under two weeks to reconcile your notices and content-marking to it before €15M / 3%-of-turnover exposure switches on. Note this is a different instrument from the still-pending Commission/EDPB guidance on the GDPR × AI Act interplay — do not conflate them.
items.source: European Commission — Shaping Europe's Digital Future

items.title: Judge grants final approval of Anthropic's $1.5B authors copyright settlement
items.summary: US District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín (San Francisco) granted final approval on 20 July to Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement with authors whose books were used to train Claude — the largest copyright settlement in US history, at roughly $3,000 per infringed work across about 500,000 titles, with objections that the sum was too low overruled. The important distinction for advisers is what this does and does not decide: it resolves the piracy/acquisition claims — that Anthropic sourced pirated copies — not the fair-use question on training itself, which an earlier ruling had treated as transformative where the underlying books were lawfully acquired. So the case does not bless or bar AI training on copyrighted works; it prices the how-you-got-the-data question, and prices it enormously. The reusable lesson for any client building or fine-tuning on a corpus is that provenance and the acquisition trail are now the litigable centre of gravity — the same point the EDPB's 8 July web-scraping guidelines make on the data-protection side. Expect this figure to become the anchor other rightsholder classes negotiate against.

items.title: DeepMind's Hassabis cites UK's evaluator experience in call for a frontier AI standards body
items.summary: In an essay published 14 July 2026, Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis proposed a US-based Frontier AI Standards Body — modelled on FINRA, industry-funded but federally overseen — to vet frontier models for dangerous capabilities before release. His argument leans on the UK's own experience: the AI Security Institute has evaluated frontier models since 2023, but roughly 32 months in, it still cannot compel a single lab to show it a model — the voluntary phase never became compulsory. The read-across for advisers is direct: a well-resourced technical evaluator without a legal power to compel disclosure functions as an advisory body, not a regulator, which is exactly the distinction the EU's own voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency has to answer for under Article 50.

items.title: Hawaii signs chatbot safety and deepfake laws as US state AI patchwork tightens
items.summary: Hawaii Governor Josh Green signed two AI bills into law on 13 July: SB 3001 requires operators of conversational AI to disclose AI status to users, build protocols against producing suicidal-ideation content, and add protections for minor account holders; HB 2137 prohibits harmful uses of digital imitations and requires disclosure of synthetic performers in advertising. The same week, Illinois signed laws barring AI from public-school teacher evaluations (SB 2909) and restricting AI in healthcare procedure approvals (SB 3114). The read-across for anyone deploying chatbots on both sides of the Atlantic: US state chatbot-disclosure duties are converging on what Article 50(1) EU AI Act requires from 2 August — a single, well-designed 'you are talking to an AI' disclosure layer now does double duty across jurisdictions, while self-harm safeguard and minor-protection duties are becoming the US state baseline with no EU equivalent to lean on.

items.title: AI Office publishes frontier-AI expert report — 'next one to two years decisive' for EU
items.summary: The EU AI Office released a report distilling input from over 100 experts on how Europe can build competitiveness, sovereignty and security in frontier AI, warning that the next one to two years are decisive if the EU is to move to a position of strength. The candid diagnosis: world-class research and talent, but frontier development concentrated overseas, and computing infrastructure and growth-stage capital not yet at the scale frontier AI requires. The line that matters for compliance advisers is the explicit call for 'legal certainty around training data in copyright and data protection' as a named barrier to growth — read alongside the 8 July EDPB scraping and anonymisation guidelines, it signals the Commission itself now treats the lawful-basis question for training data as a competitiveness problem, not just a compliance one. Not binding law and does not reflect the Commission's official position, but it maps where policy pressure and future guidance will flow.

items.title: New York enacts first US statewide AI data-centre moratorium — one-year hyperscale permit pause
items.summary: Governor Hochul signed an executive order making New York the first US state to pause permitting of new hyperscale data centres (over 50MW) for up to a year, while the Department of Environmental Conservation prepares a cumulative environmental impact assessment. A companion legislative track directs the Public Service Commission to create a separate utility rate class so AI operators pay the full cost of their own grid upgrades rather than passing them to residential ratepayers. The practical signal for anyone deploying at scale: AI compute is now a siting, energy and utility-regulation problem, not just a data-protection one — capacity, permitting timelines and power cost are becoming board-level risks in the jurisdictions hosting the infrastructure. Watch for copycat measures; the article notes a federal AI Data Center Moratorium Act is also in draft.

items.title: Nigeria forms Joint Technical Coordination Committee to build unified digital/AI framework
items.summary: Minister Bosun Tijani confirmed Nigeria will hold new digital-platform and AI rules in abeyance until a single harmonised framework exists, and has stood up a Joint Technical Coordination Committee drawing on the NCC, NITDA and NDPC to draft it. This is the constructive follow-through on the early-July postponement rather than a fresh delay — the three agencies whose overlapping mandates created the uncertainty are now being forced to speak with one voice under the Minister. For organisations with Nigerian operations or users, the takeaway is that the regime is being rebuilt to be coherent (and therefore more enforceable) rather than abandoned; the sensible move is to keep governance documentation current so you are ready when the unified rules land, rather than treating the pause as a reprieve.

items.title: CJEU C-199/24 (Legal Newsdesk Sweden): 'journalistic purposes' GDPR carve-out read narrowly
items.summary: The CJEU (Fifth Chamber) ruled on 9 July that publishing public criminal-conviction records online for a fee, without editing, adaptation, editorial policy or journalistic ethical standards, is not processing for 'journalistic purposes' under Article 85(2) GDPR — so the derogations from the GDPR's core chapters do not apply. The Court also held Member States cannot use Article 85(1) to extend those exemptions beyond journalistic/academic/artistic/literary expression, nor strip data subjects of the Chapter VIII remedies (complaint, judicial remedy, compensation). Directly relevant to AI dataset and web-scraping practice: a provider hoping to shelter a scraped corpus behind a 'journalism' or 'freedom of expression' framing now has to show genuine editorial selection, verification and professional standards — merely making public-record data searchable at scale will not qualify.
items.source: Court of Justice of the EU (C-199/24)

items.title: Digital Omnibus on AI enters into force — Annex III delay to Dec 2027 now binding law
items.summary: The Digital Omnibus on AI entered into force this week following Official Journal publication, capping the European Parliament's 16 June vote and the Council's 29 June final green light. The Annex III high-risk deadline (2 Dec 2027) and Annex I deadline (2 Aug 2028) are no longer provisional — they are now legally binding, so the 'not yet law' caveat on those dates can come off the tracker. Separately, GPAI penalty enforcement activates 2 August 2026 and applies retroactively to violations dating back to August 2025 — any foundation-model provider treating the first year as a free pass should assume past conduct is now exposed. Article 50 transparency obligations are unaffected by the high-risk delay and remain enforceable 2 August 2026 as originally scheduled.

items.title: Tinubu directs FCCPC to investigate Big Tech and generative AI platforms over news scraping
items.summary: President Tinubu has directed the FCCPC to investigate Meta, Alphabet, X and unnamed generative AI platforms over alleged unauthorised scraping of Nigerian news content for model training, following a joint petition from the Nigerian Press Organisation. This runs alongside — not instead of — the broader NITDA/NCC/NDPC digital-platform rules postponement reported 3 July: the FCCPC action targets AI training-data practices specifically under the FCCPA 2018, a competition/consumer-protection statute, not the stalled AI-specific governance framework. For any client operating AI products with Nigerian user bases or training data sourced from Nigerian media, this is a live enforcement track independent of the paused AI regulations — FCCPC has form here, having fined Meta $220M in 2025 (under appeal).

items.title: EU Parliament passes Chat Control 1.0 by default — AI-based message scanning legal to 2028
items.summary: EU Parliament passed Chat Control 1.0 into law on 9 July without a majority of MEPs ever voting for it — a second-reading procedural quirk meant the 314 votes against fell 47 short of the 361 needed to block the Council's text. The law authorises (does not mandate) voluntary scanning of unencrypted messaging and email services using AI image classifiers and grooming-detection text analysis, running until April 2028; end-to-end encrypted services such as WhatsApp and Signal stay outside scope. Relevant to any client running AI-based content moderation or trust-and-safety tooling on EU users' communications — coverage citing the Commission's own implementation data puts the AI classifiers' false-positive rate as high as 20%, a proportionality question likely headed to the CJEU.

items.title: EDPB adopts anonymisation guidelines — 'strip the names' is no longer enough
items.summary: At its 8 July plenary the EDPB adopted Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation, replacing the old 2014 working definition and folding in the CJEU ruling in C-413/23 P (EDPS v SRB, Sept 2025). Data is only anonymous if it passes three tests: no singling-out, no linkability, and no inference. The inference test is the one that bites AI — if attributes of a person can be inferred with high probability from the remaining values, the data stays personal data and GDPR applies in full, regardless of how many identifying fields you deleted. Practical take for anyone training or deploying models: the common assumption that a de-identified training set sits outside GDPR is now formally closed. Re-identification risk has to be assessed against modern attacker capability, including AI's cross-referencing and pattern-extraction power. Open for consultation to 30 October 2026.

items.title: EDPB guidelines on web scraping for generative AI: legitimate interest is not a free pass
items.summary: Alongside the anonymisation guidelines, the EDPB adopted separate guidelines on web scraping in the context of generative AI. The message to model builders is direct: scraping that touches personal data is GDPR processing (collection, storage, organisation, retrieval), so you need a lawful basis, and legitimate interest only holds up if you can evidence the balancing test, respect purpose limitation, and meet transparency and data-minimisation duties — scraping only from reliable sources, timestamping, and validating before training. Special-category data (health, politics, religion, etc.) remains prohibited in principle: incidental collection needs both an Article 6 basis and an Article 9(2) exception, with no general exemption. For any organisation building or fine-tuning on scraped data, this is the operational benchmark a supervisory authority will now measure you against. Open for consultation to 30 October 2026.

items.title: FTC proposes policy statement on AI accuracy and output steering
items.summary: The Federal Trade Commission opened a public comment period (closing 31 July) on a proposed policy statement targeting AI companies that suppress accuracy or steer outputs toward undisclosed ideological objectives. The FTC's framing: consumers expect AI systems to produce the most accurate output within technical and resource limits, and distorting outputs without disclosure violates Section 5 of the FTC Act (deceptive practices). The compliance path is clear — adequate disclosure of design objectives avoids liability. For organisations deploying AI in the US market, the practical point is that 'accuracy' is now formally treated as a consumer expectation, and steering behavior must be disclosed; the statement effectively presumes bad-faith accuracy suppression absent clear notice.

items.title: Commission presents EU Action Plan on Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence
items.summary: The European Commission published a coordinated action plan addressing AI's dual role in cybersecurity: AI tools can detect vulnerabilities and strengthen critical infrastructure, but malicious actors can exploit AI to automate attacks at scale. The Plan includes capacity-building (secure testing platforms, evaluation frameworks, ENISA-led guidance), coordination with Member States and industry, and reinforcement of existing NIS2 and Cyber Resilience Act obligations. For organisations deploying AI systems with cybersecurity implications or handling critical infrastructure, the signal is that the Commission is now treating AI-driven cyber risk as a policy priority alongside the Act's transparency and high-risk regimes — expect Member State implementations of these principles to flow through national competent authorities over the next 12 months.

items.title: Federal government postpones implementation of digital platform and AI governance rules
items.summary: The Nigerian government has directed NITDA, the NCC and the NDPC to postpone implementation of broad new regulations for digital platforms and online intermediaries. The postponement follows a presidential order directing the FCCPC to investigate major technology companies for anti-competitive practices and content exploitation. For organisations deploying AI in Nigeria, this delays the threatened 2% annual-turnover penalty regime for AI governance breaches — but the rule itself is not withdrawn, only deferred. The practical step is to complete AI governance audits and risk assessments before the rescheduled deadline, which will align with broader federal digital economy legislation timelines.

items.title: DPC Annual Report 2025: cases up 45%, AI named a core driver of complexity and risk
items.summary: The DPC published its 2025 Annual Report on 30 June. Headline numbers: 16,160 new cases (up 45% on 2024), 208 cross-border complaints concluded as EU/EEA lead authority (up 43%), and €530.77M in fines across four large-scale inquiries — dominated by the €530M TikTok China-transfers decision. The Chairperson singled out AI twice: complainants are using AI tools to generate voluminous, complex submissions, and the scale of personal-data processing by advancing AI systems has 'heightened risks and harms for individuals.' Read the signal: the regulator now co-supervising AI under S.I. 366/2025 is telling deployers that GDPR exposure and AI Act exposure will be assessed together. If your AI system touches personal data, your DPIA and lawful-basis documentation are the first thing an Irish investigator will ask for.

items.title: NITDA defends 2% turnover penalty for AI non-compliance amid 'innovation tax' backlash
items.summary: NITDA's proposed 2026 digital governance framework includes a 2% annual-turnover penalty for breach of emerging AI governance standards — and the startup ecosystem is pushing back hard, warning of capital flight and developer emigration. NITDA's response is notable: it explicitly frames the penalty as alignment with international practice (transparency, auditing, financial sanctions), which reads as EU AI Act-style enforcement architecture arriving in Nigeria. For any organisation deploying AI with Nigerian operations or users, the practical point is that percentage-of-turnover penalty exposure is no longer an EU-only concept — and 'compliance requirements subject to interpretation' is precisely the gap a documented governance programme closes.

items.title: GDPR fines top €7.1B: AI processing named top enforcement trigger for H2 2026
items.summary: A mid-year enforcement analysis drawing on DLA Piper data confirms GDPR fines have exceeded €7.1 billion cumulatively, with €600 million issued in H1 2026 alone and 443 breach notifications arriving daily — a 22% year-on-year rise. Supervisory authorities are moving down-market: a €27M fine on Free Mobile (security failures), £14.5M on Reddit (age-verification gaps), and €200K on Kaspr (consent-free data scraping) show ordinary businesses are now firmly in scope. AI processing is identified as the highest-growth enforcement trigger for H2 2026 — organisations that trained models or deployed automated decision-making without a documented lawful basis, updated transparency notices, or completed DPIAs face overlapping exposure under both GDPR Article 5 and the EU AI Act. The Article 22 right against automated decisions adds a further layer for any system influencing credit, hiring, or pricing.

items.title: Sidley: AI Omnibus key provisions — registration reinstated, safety component narrowed
items.summary: Sidley Austin's post-Parliament analysis flags two Omnibus changes not widely reported: the registration obligation for AI systems relying on the Article 6(3) exemption (narrow procedural task) has been reinstated — providers must still register the system, via a simplified procedure. Separately, the 'safety component' definition under Article 6(1) has been narrowed so that AI assisting users or optimising performance is not automatically high-risk unless failure creates actual health or safety risk. The AI literacy duty has also been softened from a direct provider/deployer obligation to a Commission and Member State obligation to 'support and facilitate.' Council formal adoption remains pending, with both institutions targeting completion before 2 August 2026.

items.title: Commission publishes Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content
items.summary: The European Commission published the final Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content on 10 June 2026 — the practical compliance instrument for Article 50 obligations taking effect 2 August 2026. The Code is voluntary and sets a multi-layered approach: signatories must use at least two technical marking methods (e.g. metadata plus watermark) where no single technique suffices. Deepfakes and AI-manipulated content on matters of public interest must be clearly labelled; providers of chatbots must disclose AI interaction to users. For systems placed on market before 2 August 2026, a transitional compliance period runs to 2 December 2026. Any organisation deploying generative AI — image, video, audio, or text — should treat this Code as the operational implementation guide for Article 50.

items.title: Irish AI Office stripped of market surveillance authority role in published Bill
items.summary: William Fry analysis of the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill 2026 (published 17 June) confirms a significant departure from the General Scheme: the AI Office of Ireland will not hold a designation as a market surveillance authority (MSA). Instead, it is confined to coordination, single point of contact, and the national register and sandbox. Front-line investigation and enforcement sit with the 15 sectoral regulators designated under S.I. No. 366 of 2025. William Fry flags a potential Article 70(2) compliance issue — that provision requires the single point of contact to be an MSA. For organisations, the practical consequence is that the competent authority they engage with on substantive AI compliance will be their sectoral regulator (Central Bank, DPC, CCPC, etc.), not the AI Office. Bill is not yet finalised; further amendments expected through the Oireachtas.

items.title: EDPB launches contact form to flag GDPR interpretation inconsistencies
items.summary: The European Data Protection Board launched a dedicated contact form on 24 June 2026 enabling any stakeholder to flag possible inconsistencies in how the GDPR is interpreted across the EU — including divergences between national supervisory authorities, and between national positions and the EDPB's own guidance. The EDPB will not respond to individual submissions, but will compile and discuss reports at Board level to consider steps to improve consistency. Based on the EDPB Helsinki Statement on enhanced clarity, support and engagement. Directly relevant to organisations operating across multiple EU jurisdictions, and to any cross-border AI data processing programme where national supervisory authority positions on GDPR obligations may diverge. Contact form: edpb.europa.eu/contact/flag-an-inconsistency

items.title: AI Omnibus adopted by Parliament — Council vote expected 29 June
items.summary: The European Parliament adopted the Digital Omnibus on AI on 16 June by 423 votes to 57, formally locking in the May 7 trilogue deal. Three steps remain: Council formal adoption (expected 29 June), presidential signature, and Official Journal publication. Until OJ publication, the original AI Act dates remain the legal baseline — organisations mapping Annex III systems should still treat August 2 as real. The vote also fixed application dates as calendar certainties, replacing the conditional trigger tied to technical standards. Watermarking under Article 50 and the nudifier/CSAM ban still take effect 2 December 2026.

items.title: High-risk AI classification consultation extended to 23 July 2026
items.summary: The Commission extended the targeted consultation on its draft guidelines for classifying high-risk AI systems from 23 June to 23 July 2026, following stakeholder requests for more time. The guidelines clarify how Articles 6(1) and 6(2) of the AI Act apply — including the 'safety component' test and Annex III use-case mapping — and will be finalised by end of 2026. Any organisation still working through whether its AI systems are high-risk now has an additional four weeks to engage. Submissions via the EU Survey questionnaire linked on the consultation page.

items.title: Digital Omnibus: high-risk AI deadlines pushed back
items.summary: Council and Parliament reached provisional political agreement on the 'Digital Omnibus' — the first amendments to the AI Act. Annex III high-risk obligations move from Aug 2026 to Dec 2027; Annex I (product-embedded) from Aug 2027 to Aug 2028. SME-style simplified compliance extended to firms up to 750 staff / €150m revenue. Formal adoption expected before 2 August 2026.

items.title: ICO's statutory duty to write an AI and automated-decision-making Code of Practice takes effect
items.summary: The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/425) came into force on 12 May 2026, placing the Information Commissioner's Office under a statutory duty to produce a Code of Practice on AI and automated decision-making, including specific guidance on children's personal data. The ICO's consultation on draft non-statutory guidance — reflecting the Data (Use and Access) Act's Article 22A–22D reforms — closed 29 May 2026, with the final Code, expected later in 2026, set to carry binding legal weight once published, unlike the EU's voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency. For any organisation processing UK personal data through automated decisions or AI, this Code will become the first document a UK regulator reaches for — the same role DPIA and lawful-basis documentation already play for the DPC in Ireland.

items.title: Draft high-risk classification guidelines published
items.summary: The European Commission released draft guidelines on classifying high-risk AI systems and opened a public consultation (closed 23 June 2026). Important reference for any organisation scoping Annex III obligations — the guidelines clarify the 'safety component' test and when an AI system embedded in a product triggers the high-risk regime.

items.title: New Article 5 prohibition on 'nudifier' apps and CSAM
items.summary: The Omnibus adds a prohibition (effective 2 December 2026) on AI systems generating non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material — a notable expansion of the Act's banned-practices list beyond what was in the original 2024 text.

items.title: Regulation of AI Bill 2026 formally published
items.summary: The Irish Government formally published the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill 2026, moving beyond the February General Scheme. The Bill establishes Oifig IS na hÉireann (AI Office of Ireland) as an independent statutory market-surveillance authority, a single point of contact for the EU AI Act, and a national hub for AI expertise — all operational by 1 August 2026.
items.source: Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment

items.title: National Digital & AI Strategy 2030 launched
items.summary: 'Digital Ireland – Connecting our People, Securing our Future' published; the Data Protection Commission, via the Digital Regulators Group, confirmed its continuing oversight of personal-data processing in AI, including within regulatory sandboxes — making clear that GDPR obligations run in parallel with AI Act compliance.

items.title: Great American AI Act: first comprehensive federal AI governance draft
items.summary: Representatives Obernolte and Trahan released a 269-page bipartisan discussion draft proposing the first comprehensive federal AI framework in the US. Key provisions include mandatory registration and third-party audits for frontier model developers, whistleblower protections, and — most controversially — a three-year moratorium on conflicting state AI laws, directly targeting the patchwork of state rules in Colorado, California, and roughly 30 other states.

items.title: EO: Promoting Advanced AI Innovation and Security
items.summary: President Trump signed an executive order establishing new cybersecurity mandates and a voluntary framework for secure deployment of frontier AI models — reinforcing the administration's position that AI innovation must not be stifled by excessive regulation, while requiring agencies to increase scrutiny of AI-enabled cyber threats.

items.title: Colorado repeals landmark AI law, replaces with narrower statute
items.summary: Colorado's comprehensive AI Act — originally due in force 30 June 2026 — was repealed in May 2026 and replaced with SB 26-189, a narrower statute regulating automated decision-making technology effective January 2027. A significant retreat driven in part by industry pressure and the White House's federal preemption push.

items.title: White House blueprint: federal preemption of state AI laws
items.summary: The White House released a National Policy Framework for AI directing Congress to adopt a unified federal approach and challenging state AI laws seen as inconsistent with federal policy — setting up a sustained federal-versus-state conflict that is reshaping the US AI compliance landscape.

items.title: Digital Economy & E-Governance Bill: AI provisions advance
items.summary: Nigeria's National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill — anticipated for passage in Q2 2026 — would grant NITDA authority to classify AI systems by risk, mandate algorithmic transparency and annual audits for high-risk deployments, and require developer licences. Fines of up to NGN 10m or 2% of annual Nigerian revenue would apply, potentially making Nigeria the first African country with a comprehensive, enforceable AI regime.

items.title: Regulation of AI Bill 2026 completes Seanad Second Stage, now in Committee Stage
items.summary: The Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill 2026 completed Seanad Second Stage on 1 July 2026 and is now progressing through Seanad Committee Stage. The Bill previously completed Dáil Second Stage (24 June) and Committee/Remaining Stages (30 June). No substantive changes to the AI Office of Ireland structure or Market Surveillance Authority allocation reported at this stage.

items.title: Nigeria's Supreme Court launches digital case management; e-filing now mandatory
items.summary: The Chief Justice of Nigeria launched the Nigerian Case Management System (NCMS) on 1 July, with new Practice Directions making electronic upload of court documents mandatory for Supreme Court appeals. The system creates secure digital repositories and audit trails for filings — and the CJN paired the launch with a direct warning: uploading forged or altered documents will attract legal and disciplinary sanctions. NBA President Afam Osigwe pledged the Bar's support and urged practitioners to embrace the transition. For Nigerian practitioners the compliance point is immediate — mandatory e-filing is now a professional-conduct issue, not an optional convenience, and document integrity in the digital registry will be auditable.

items.title: NBA Birnin Kebbi Law Week: AI and the legal profession
items.summary: The NBA Birnin Kebbi Branch published its full report on the 'Justice Beyond Algorithms' Law Week, covering panel sessions on AI's impact on justice delivery and the legal profession in Nigeria — including ethics, liability, and whether current Nigerian law is equipped to regulate AI decision-making in courts.

items.title: AI Growth Lab launches — legal services named first sandbox sector
items.summary: The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology launched the UK's AI Growth Lab in June 2026 — an advisory regulatory sandbox letting AI products undergo supervised real-world testing with rules temporarily relaxed for licensed pilots. Legal services and conveyancing were named the first participating sector, with the Legal Services Board, Solicitors Regulation Authority, Council for Licensed Conveyancers and Information Commissioner's Office all named as participating regulators; applications for legal-sector participants were expected to open later in the summer, with healthcare, transport and advanced manufacturing to follow through 2026–2027. This is the UK's practical answer to the EU's Annex III risk-classification debate: rather than a horizontal statute, it is testing AI governance sector by sector, with the legal profession itself as the first live experiment — directly relevant to any UK-facing legal-tech deployment or firm considering the sandbox route.

items.title: NBA-SBL 20th Annual Conference features AI adoption agenda
items.summary: The NBA Section on Business Law held its 20th Annual International Business Law Conference in Abuja from 8–10 June 2026, themed 'Beyond Reforms: Measuring Policy Impact'. A dedicated pre-conference webinar on AI adoption in Nigerian legal practice — covering competence duties, liability, and governance — marked AI tools as a mainstream agenda item at Nigeria's premier business law gathering.

items.title: NBA Lagos Law Week: 'Lawyering in the Digital Age'
items.summary: The NBA Lagos Branch announced its 2026 Law Week — running 27 June to 3 July — themed 'Lawyering in the Digital Age: Navigating Technology, Justice and Innovation'. The event signals growing Bar-level recognition that Nigerian legal practice must systematically address AI tools, digital evidence, and tech-driven disputes.

items.title: NBA President directive on technology utilisation
items.summary: The NBA President issued a directive to all branches on membership participation, technology utilisation and branch elections — part of a wider push to modernise the Bar's digital operations and ensure branches engage with the growing AI and digital agenda at national level.

items.title: Midjourney ordered to produce evidence of studio AI use in copyright discovery
items.summary: In the ongoing copyright class action filed by Warner Bros. Discovery, Disney and Universal against Midjourney, a US District Court ordered Midjourney to submit detailed information about each studio's internal use of AI tools. This discovery victory for plaintiffs directly undermines Midjourney's fair-use defence (that training on publicly available images is standard practice) if the studios' own AI applications rely on identical methods. This case remains the highest-profile AI copyright litigation in the US and is shaping discovery precedent for 70+ pending AI copyright suits — discovery outcomes here will influence settlements and trial strategies across the entire docket.

items.title: CJEU — NTH Haustechnik: GDPR-obtained evidence admissible in civil proceedings
items.summary: CJEU, 18 June 2026 (C-484/24). Courts processing documents containing personal data are themselves subject to GDPR — but evidence obtained in breach of data protection law is not automatically inadmissible. Courts must balance GDPR obligations against the right to a fair hearing. The two questions (was data collected unlawfully, and may the court use it) are distinct. Direct relevance to AI audit logs, Article 12 logging obligations, and AI-generated evidence in commercial disputes.

items.title: TikTok v DPC — Irish High Court upholds €530M GDPR fine
items.summary: Irish High Court, 3 June 2026. Court upheld the DPC's €530M GDPR fine on TikTok's transfers of EEA user data to China but ordered the DPC to reconsider the corrective order suspending future transfers. DPC confirmed it will not appeal. Live precedent: Standard Contractual Clauses plus supplementary measures cannot bridge a conflict with Chinese intelligence law. The DPC's transfer analysis now has High Court backing — directly relevant to any Irish/EU business relying on SCCs for AI data flows to third countries.

items.title: Court of Rome annuls Garante's €15M OpenAI fine — DPC now leads
items.summary: Tribunale di Roma, 18 March 2026 (R.G. 4785/2025). Italy's €15M GDPR fine against OpenAI annulled: once OpenAI's Irish establishment was recognised (February 2024), the Garante lost competence under the Article 56 one-stop-shop mechanism. The DPC became lead supervisory authority. Every substantive violation found — no legal basis for training data, transparency failures, age-verification failures — was never examined on the merits. Ireland is now the de-facto lead GDPR enforcer for AI companies in the EU.

items.title: CJEU — Dun & Bradstreet: automated decisions require genuine explanation
items.summary: CJEU, 27 February 2025 (C-203/22). Under Article 22 GDPR, data controllers must provide a genuine, intelligible explanation of the logic of automated decisions — handing over the algorithm or a complex formula does not suffice. Where a controller claims trade-secret protection for its AI model, the supervisory authority or court adjudicates the balance. Directly relevant to any AI system making or materially influencing decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

items.title: Thomson Reuters v. Ross: first appellate AI fair-use argument
items.summary: The US Third Circuit Court of Appeals heard oral argument on 11 June 2026 in Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence — the first appellate-level consideration of whether training an AI system on copyrighted works constitutes fair use. The ruling will set binding precedent in the Third Circuit and is widely expected to influence the broader wave of AI copyright litigation against OpenAI, Meta and others.

items.title: Authors v. OpenAI: court affirms 20M ChatGPT logs order
items.summary: Judge Sidney Stein affirmed the order compelling OpenAI to produce 20 million anonymised ChatGPT conversation logs to plaintiffs in the consolidated copyright MDL — rejecting OpenAI's attempt to narrow production to logs mentioning only the specific works at issue. A critical discovery milestone with implications for how AI output similarity will be assessed at trial.

items.title: US Supreme Court declines Thaler AI-authorship appeal
items.summary: The Supreme Court denied certiorari in Dr Stephen Thaler's case, leaving intact the principle that copyright requires human authorship — AI-generated works without a human creative contributor are not registrable. The decision closes the door on autonomous-AI authorship claims in the US for the foreseeable future.

items.title: Kadrey v. Meta: fair-use motion partially granted
items.summary: In the consolidated copyright litigation against Meta, the court granted a partial motion to dismiss on fair-use grounds for training the Llama LLM — but allowed claims related to alleged reproduction of pirated works during the 'seeding' stage to proceed. Signals that AI training on legitimately held copies may get more protection than training via torrented content.

items.title: Germany's KI-MIG clears the Bundesrat — Bundesnetzagentur confirmed as AI Act enforcer
items.summary: Germany's AI Market Surveillance and Innovation Promotion Act (KI-MIG) — the national statute standing up enforcement behind the directly-applicable AI Act — cleared its final legislative hurdle on 10 July 2026, when the Bundesrat declined to call the mediation committee, following the Bundestag's 11 June vote and February Cabinet approval. Germany had already missed the Act's original August 2025 deadline to designate a market surveillance authority; KI-MIG closes that gap just in time for 2 August. The Bundesnetzagentur (Federal Network Agency) becomes the default AI market surveillance authority, single point of contact for the EU AI Office, and central complaints office, with a new coordination unit (KoKIVO) and an independent chamber (UKIM) for the most rights-sensitive cases. Sector regulators keep their own lanes — BaFin for finance, Länder authorities for education, policing, justice and social-benefits AI — while fines up to €35M/7% of global turnover route through ordinary local courts (Amtsgerichte), a first-instance forum commentators already call under-resourced for cases of this size. For any client with German operations, the Bundesnetzagentur is now the concrete address for AI Act compliance questions, not just Brussels.
items.source: Legal Tribune Online (Prof. Dr. Karsten Löw)

items.title: CNIL and CIANum flag agentic AI as a new front in GDPR risk
items.summary: France's data protection authority and the Conseil de l'IA générative et du Numérique (CIANum) published a joint exploratory note on 20 July 2026 on what agentic AI — systems with decision-making autonomy, persistent memory, and the ability to act across multiple services on a user's behalf — does to core GDPR concepts. The concern: purpose limitation strains when an agent chains actions the original consent never contemplated, data minimisation strains when an agent needs broad tool access to complete an open-ended task, and accountability blurs when the system, not a human, initiates the processing step. Non-binding, framed as early joint reflection rather than guidance, but it is the first authority-level French signal that agent autonomy — not just model training — is now a live compliance surface, arriving as agentic products move from labs into ordinary business workflows. Worth tracking alongside the EDPB's 8 July anonymisation and scraping guidelines as the next wave of GDPR-AI interpretation.

items.title: Munich court holds OpenAI directly liable for AI memorisation of copyrighted lyrics — GEMA v OpenAI
items.summary: Munich Regional Court I (case no. 42 O 14139/24) ruled on 11 November 2025 that ChatGPT's storage of nine well-known German song lyrics inside its model parameters ('memorisation') and their reproduction in chatbot output ('regurgitation') infringes the reproduction right under s.16 of the German Copyright Act (UrhG) — the first European court to hold an AI developer directly liable for training-data copyright infringement, rather than merely for how the data was acquired. The court found the EU/German text-and-data-mining exception does not shelter this kind of output-level reproduction, and granted GEMA's claim for injunctive relief, information disclosure and damages. OpenAI has confirmed it will appeal to the Munich Court of Appeal (OLG München), expected to rule in 2026 and set the first EU appellate-level precedent on generative AI training and copyright. Directly relevant to any client relying on a TDM exception for an EU-facing model: this ruling treats the output, not just the ingestion, as the point of infringement.
items.source: Norton Rose Fulbright / Munich Regional Court I

items.title: GEMA v Suno verdict now due 31 July — second Munich test of AI-music liability
items.summary: The same Munich Regional Court that decided GEMA v OpenAI is due to rule on GEMA's parallel copyright claim against AI-music platform Suno (case no. 42 O 763/25) on 31 July 2026 — one day before the AI Act's own 2 August deadline. The court heard the case on 9 March 2026; GEMA's evidence centres on Suno outputs it says are 'misleadingly similar' to specific copyrighted songs in melody, harmony and rhythm. The court has postponed the judgment once already (from 12 June to 31 July) without signalling an outcome either way. A finding for GEMA would be the first European ruling requiring a generative AI music platform to licence the catalogue it trained on, reinforcing the direct-liability approach the same court took against OpenAI. Two Munich-driven data points on AI liability landing in the same window as the Article 50 deadline — worth citing together in any August advisory content.

items.title: Conseil d'État bars algorithmic video surveillance at Nice schools — no legal basis under current law
items.summary: France's highest administrative court confirmed on 30 January 2026 the CNIL's May 2025 opinion that Nice's 'zone d'intrusion' system — real-time algorithmic detection of vehicles parked illegally outside school entrances, built on standard public-space CCTV — has no legal basis. The Code de la sécurité intérieure permits video surveillance of public space but does not authorise systematic, automated algorithmic analysis of the footage collected; any future deployment would need a specific law passed by Parliament, not an extension of existing camera authority. The mayor of Nice publicly objected that the ruling blocks municipalities from using available technology to protect residents. The read-across for AI Act Article 5/Annex III scoping anywhere in the EU: French courts are treating 'we already have lawful CCTV' as no answer to 'did you get separate legal authority for the algorithm analysing it' — a distinction likely to recur wherever public-sector AI is bolted onto existing surveillance infrastructure.

items.title: France still has not designated its AI Act competent authorities, five months past deadline
items.summary: France published a draft designation of 17 AI Act market surveillance authorities on 9 September 2025 — CNIL (data/biometric use cases), DGCCRF (consumer/competition, coordination lead) and Arcom (audiovisual) carrying most of the load, backed by a shared technical-expertise pool drawing on ANSSI and PEReN. But the provisions formalising this designation were withdrawn from the DDADUE EU-adaptation bill before it reached Parliament, and as of this note France remains one of the EU member states with no legally designated competent authority — five months past the Act's own August 2025 deadline. Practical consequence for any organisation with French AI operations: the proposed regulator map (which authority you'd actually deal with on an enforcement question) is not yet law — treat CNIL/DGCCRF/Arcom oversight as the working assumption, not a confirmed designation, until the decree lands.
items.source: MIAI — Chair AI Regulation, Grenoble Alpes

items.title: CJEU holds first-ever hearing on generative AI and copyright — Like Company v Google
items.summary: The CJEU held its first-ever oral hearing on generative AI and EU copyright law on 10 March 2026, in a Hungarian preliminary reference, Like Company v Google Ireland (C-250/25). A Hungarian press publisher argues Google's Gemini chatbot reproduces and communicates its editorial content to the public without authorisation when it answers questions using near-identical text. The referred questions go to the core of LLM copyright exposure: whether a chatbot displaying content substantially identical to a protected publication performs an 'act of communication to the public,' and how EU copyright's territorial scope applies to a model trained and queried across borders. No ruling yet — an Advocate General opinion is expected first — but this is the case that will set the EU-wide answer that the German GEMA rulings and the pending Article 50 guidance are all currently working around on a national-borders basis. Any client relying on a single-jurisdiction AI training/output analysis should treat this as the one to watch before finalising a cross-border position.

items.title: Nanterre court: French works council consultation duty applies even to AI 'pilots'
items.summary: In the first French court ruling on AI deployment in the workplace, the Nanterre Court of Justice held on 14 February 2025 (N° RG 24/01457) that a company's AI rollout — presented internally as a mere 'pilot' — had in fact reached the works council's consultation trigger, because several tools (including Finovox and Synthesia) were already in live use by all affected staff. The court ordered the project suspended pending consultation, under a €1,000-per-day penalty, plus €5,000 in damages — rejecting the employer's argument that experimentation falls outside the works council's Article L.2312-8 'new technology' consultation right. The lesson generalises past France: under Recital 92 AI Act and equivalent EU worker-information duties, calling a deployment a 'pilot' does not exempt it from consultation obligations once real employees are actually using the tool — the legal test tracks actual use, not the label management puts on the rollout phase.
